t: Maximum Split of Positive Even Integers: Greedy Smallest-First Splitting
o: finalSum must be partitioned into distinct positive even integers, using as many parts as possible. For finalSum = 12 the split 2 + 4 + 6 uses three parts and is optimal; for odd finalSum = 7 no split exists at all, because any sum of even numbers is even. For finalSum = 28 a maximum split has four parts, for instance 2 + 4 + 6 + 16 — the sample answer 6 + 8 + 2 + 12 is equally valid, since any split reaching the maximum count is accepted. With finalSum up to 10^10 we cannot explore subsets, but greedily consuming the smallest unused evens 2, 4, 6, ... produces at most about sqrt(finalSum) parts, which keeps the work tiny.
k: A sum of even integers is even, so an odd finalSum has no valid split.
To maximize the number of parts, spend the smallest distinct evens first — each additional part then costs as little sum as possible.
After taking 2 + 4 + ... + 2k, any leftover is even and smaller than the next candidate 2(k+1); folding it into the largest part preserves uniqueness.

a.n: Approach 1: Greedy Over Ascending Even Numbers
a.i: Using the smallest available values maximizes the count of parts: swapping any part for a smaller unused even number never decreases the count. Sweep cur = 2, 4, 6, ... appending each value while it still fits into the remaining sum. Whatever remains afterward is strictly smaller than the next candidate, so adding it to the last (largest) part keeps all parts unique while preserving the total.
s: If finalSum is odd, return an empty list.
Set cur = 2 and initialize an empty result list.
While finalSum >= cur, append cur, subtract it from finalSum, and increase cur by 2.
If any remainder remains, add it to the last appended value.
a.t: O(sqrt(finalSum)) — the parts 2, 4, ..., 2k sum to k(k+1), so at most about sqrt(finalSum) iterations occur.
a.sp: O(1) extra space beyond the output list.

a.n: Approach 2: Closed-Form Part Count, Then Distribute
a.i: The greedy loop can be replaced by algebra: the first k distinct evens sum to k(k+1), so the largest feasible k is the biggest integer with k(k+1) <= finalSum, obtainable from the quadratic formula with small integer corrections against floating-point error. Emit 2, 4, ..., 2k and pour the even remainder finalSum - k(k+1), which is necessarily less than 2(k+1), into the last part; the enlarged part then exceeds every other part, keeping uniqueness.
s: If finalSum is odd, return an empty list.
Find the maximum k with k(k+1) <= finalSum via the quadratic formula plus adjustment loops.
Add the remainder finalSum - k(k+1) to the last output value.
a.t: O(sqrt(finalSum)) — dominated by emitting the k output parts; locating k costs O(1).
a.sp: O(1) extra space beyond the output list.

w: Present the greedy in an interview — smallest-first is provably count-optimal because every extra part consumes the least possible remaining sum — and mention that the judge accepts any split achieving the maximum count. Classic pitfalls: skipping the parity check (odd input returns []), and appending the leftover as a new part instead of merging it into the largest part, which risks duplicating an existing value. All arithmetic needs 64-bit types since finalSum reaches 10^10. Edge cases: finalSum = 2 returns [2], and finalSum = 4 returns [4]. A neat follow-up is the same problem restricted to distinct odd parts, where an identical strategy applies after checking parity.
